locator: p.4, Weekly drinking guideline, applicability line
text: This applies to adults who drink regularly or frequently i.e. most weeks

locator: p.4, Weekly drinking guideline, lead-in sentence
text: The Chief Medical Officers’ guideline for both men and women is that
To keep health risks from alcohol to a low level it is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis.

If you regularly drink as much as 14 units per week, it is best to spread your drinking evenly over 3 or more days. If you have one or two heavy drinking episodes a week, you increase your risks of death from long term illness and from accidents and injuries.

The health harms from regular drinking of alcohol can develop over many years. This occurs either from the repeated risk of acute harms (e.g. alcohol-related accidents) or from long term diseases caused by alcohol, which may take ten to twenty years to develop. These illnesses, including various cancers, strokes, heart disease, liver disease, and damage to the brain and nervous system, can develop despite drinking for years without any apparent harm.

The expert group was also clear that there are a number of serious diseases, including certain cancers, which can occur even when drinking within the weekly guideline. Whilst they judge the risks to be low, this means there is no level of regular drinking that can be considered as completely safe in relation to some cancers. People can reduce these risks by drinking less than the guidelines or by not drinking at all.
If you are pregnant or think you could become pregnant, the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all, to keep risks to your baby to a minimum.

section: Symptoms of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
locator: Symptoms of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease does not usually cause any symptoms.

section: Symptoms of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
locator: Symptoms of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
text: Many people have it without realising. It's usually found when you have tests for another reason.

section: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself
locator: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself
text: If you have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, healthy lifestyle changes can reduce the build-up of fat in your liver and help repair any damage or stop it getting worse. Your GP can give you advice about this.

section: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Do)
locator: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Do)
text: exercise regularly – aim to do at least 150 minutes of exercise a week

section: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Do)
locator: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Do)
text: lose weight if you're overweight

section: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Don't)
locator: How you can treat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease yourself (Don't)
text: do not drink too much alcohol – keep to the recommended limit of no more than 14 alcohol units a week

section: Treatment for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease from a GP or specialist
locator: Treatment for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease from a GP or specialist
text: You should have check-ups as least once a year and tests every 2 to 3 years to monitor your condition.
If you stop drinking, your liver can often recover.

section: Stages of ARLD table: Stage 3, alcohol-related cirrhosis
locator: Stages of ARLD table: Stage 3, alcohol-related cirrhosis
text: The most serious stage of alcohol-related liver disease. The liver is badly damaged and scarred, and this damage cannot usually be reversed.

section: Treatment for alcohol-related liver disease (Important box)
locator: Treatment for alcohol-related liver disease (Important box)
text: If you regularly drink too much alcohol it can be very dangerous to stop drinking suddenly. Get medical help before you try to stop drinking.

section: When and where to get medical help (Immediate action required box)
locator: When and where to get medical help (Immediate action required box)
text: Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: You're worried alcohol may be affecting your liver and: you vomit blood or your poo is black and looks sticky
Most people with hepatitis C do not have any symptoms.
You can get hepatitis C if the blood from an infected person gets into your bloodstream.
You cannot get hepatitis C by hugging, kissing or sharing food or drink with someone.
If your result shows you do not have hepatitis C, you may be advised to get tested again in 6 months. This is because the test is not always accurate if you were infected recently.
Treatment can cure hepatitis C infections in most people.
Hepatitis C is treated with antiviral tablets you take every day for 8 to 12 weeks. It's important to finish your treatment for it to work.

section: How to prevent hepatitis B: Hepatitis B vaccination
locator: How to prevent hepatitis B: Hepatitis B vaccination
text: Vaccination is the best way to prevent hepatitis B. In the UK, the hepatitis B vaccine is given to babies as part of the 6-in-1 vaccine.
There is no known cure for chronic hepatitis B. It's usually treated with antivirals, and medicine to help control the virus and relieve symptoms such as itchiness, pain and sickness.
You will also need to see a liver specialist for regular check-ups.
Jaundice is when your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow. It can be a sign of something serious, such as liver disease, so you need to get urgent medical help.
Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if: your skin or the white part of your eyes look yellow
